name: Pali
confidence_why: Three independent standard grammars (Warder 1963, Geiger/Norman 1994, Oberlies 2001) agree that no Pali stress has been transmitted and that quantity, not stress, organises the language, so not determinable from the sources is the clear winner; but Jacobi 1913 positively claims for Pali an intensity accent governed by penult weight, and Geiger's own sec. 4 calls a Sanskritic-type accent 'more likely', so there is a mild, century-old, hedged dissent about the type of system rather than a clean consensus, which is the rubric's 'older source against a modern reference grammar, still a clear winner' case.

sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for Pali (pali1273, catalog kind not determinable, deciding sources Geiger 1916/1943 sec. 4 and Warder p. 4): Jacobi 1913, IF 31: 211-221. It is squarely about Pali word accent (title: '..und über die Betonung in diesen Sprachen'). Public-domain scans of the volume are open on archive.org; I downloaded the Berlin/UofT scan (whole-volume PDF and scanned), extracted the article as an 11-page PDF, cross-checked the scanned against the Digital Library of India scan and against rendered page scan of pp. 218-219, and ledgered everything in (plus an addendum). Reading: Jacobi argues from ca. 75 Pali and 180 Jaina-Prakrit sandhi cases that Pali had an expiratory an earlier reading accent dependent on the quantity of the penult (heavy penult accented, Latin-like, following Bühler on modern Sanskrit pronunciation), but he leaves the exact placement conditions open (p. 221) and notes evidence for accented long finals and an initial 'Aufton' (p. 220). This is the primary source behind the Geiger sec. 4 hedge the catalog already quotes; it REFINES rather than contradicts the not determinable coding (a hedged internal reconstruction, later set aside by von Hinüber sec. 159 / Oberlies 2001 p. 17 n. 2, is the only positive claim on record). Suggested action: add Jacobi 1913 to the per-language bibliography (it was not already listed) and cite it in the record note as the source of the 'Sanskritic/Latin-type accent' hypothesis; no change to the classification. Nothing left unread; acquisition priority none. Related leads seen only as citations inside the article (not downloaded, not in the list of works with stress in the title): Jacobi 1893, ZDMG 47: 574ff. ('Die Betonung im klassischen Sanskrit und in den Prakritsprachen'); Jacobi, KZ 35: 578ff; Pischel, KZ 34: 568ff., 35: 140ff. and Grammatik der Prakrit-Sprachen sec. 46; Grierson, ZDMG 49: 395ff.org's search API and direct downloads only; the de Gruyter DOI landing page could not be reached by automated download and was not needed.

new_statements.quote: Die Reduktionen, die im Nachlaute schwerer Pänultima eintreten, sind zweifellos durch einen expiratorischen Akzent verursacht, der auf der vorletzten Silbe liegt. Und darin liegt die eigentliche Bedeutung der von mir gemachten Beobachtungen, daß nunmehr der Charakter der Betonung im Pāli und Prakrit der Jainas als Intensitätsbetonung (Iktusakzent), und ein Hauptprinzip derselben, nämlich die Abhängigkeit dieses Iktusakzentes von der Quantität der vorletzten Silbe, unzweifelhaft festgestellt sind. [...] Es muß weiterer Untersuchung überlassen bleiben, die genaueren Bedingungen ausfindig zu machen, von denen die Stelle des Iktusakzentes im Pāli und Prakrit abhing.
new_statements.translation: The reductions that occur in the wake of a heavy penult are without doubt caused by an expiratory accent lying on the penultimate syllable. And therein lies the real significance of my observations: that the character of accentuation in Pali and Jaina Prakrit as intensity accentuation (ictus accent), and one main principle of it, namely the dependence of this ictus accent on the quantity of the penultimate syllable, are now established beyond doubt. [...] It must be left to further investigation to find out the more precise conditions on which the position of the ictus accent in Pali and Prakrit depended.
new_statements.citation: Jacobi, Hermann. 1913. Über eine neue Sandhiregel im Pāli und im Prakrit der Jainas und über die Betonung in diesen Sprachen. Indogermanische Forschungen 31: 211-221.
new_statements.locator: pp. 218-219 (end of p. 218 running onto p. 219); hedge at p. 221
new_statements.reading: Jacobi reconstructs, from sandhi vowel reductions in the canonical texts, a quantity-sensitive stress (an earlier reading) accent for Pali: a heavy penult attracts the accent, in the manner of Latin. He explicitly does not state a complete placement rule (what happens after a light penult, whether long finals are accented, an initial-syllable secondary prominence), and says so at p. 221. It is an internal-reconstruction hypothesis about a dead literary language, not a description of a transmitted or observed pronunciation. It is the primary source behind the 'as Jacobi has suggested' clause in Geiger sec. 4 that the catalog already quotes, so it makes the catalog's not determinable coding better-founded and more precise: the only positive claim on record is a hedged reconstruction of a weight-sensitive (heavy-penult) an earlier reading, contested by Pischel (Grammatik der Prakrit-Sprachen sec. 46) and later dismissed as irrelevant to MIA phonology by von Hinüber sec. 159 / Oberlies 2001 p. 17 n. 2 (already held).

tone_statements.citation: Warder, A. K. 1967. Pali Metre: A Contribution to the History of Indian Literature. London: Pali Text Society (Luzac). xxvii+252 pp. [reprinted Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 2016]. Ch. III 'Scansion', section 'Accent', secs. 71-83, pp. 55-63.
tone_statements.quote: In the Vedic language there appears to be no connection between the pitch accent, or “tone”, and metrical rhythm. A great deal of discussion has taken place, however, on the question of whether, and, if so, when, a stress accent replaced the Vedic accent at some time during the development of the Indo-Aryan languages after the Vedic period. ... If we accept a penultimate stress accent in Pali, with a secondary initial stress, we next have to take up the question whether this new accent system played any part in versification. ... The new stress accent was in Pali apparently not sufficiently felt by the poets to impose a conscious, or even an unconscious, putting together of stress and ictus.
tone_statements.locator: Ch. III 'Scansion', section 'Accent': sec. 71 p. 55; sec. 77 p. 59; sec. 82 p. 62 (also sec. 73-76 pp. 56-59 and n. 1 to sec. 112)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone stated for Pali: the Vedic pitch accent ('tone', musical accent) is treated as replaced, by the Pali period, by a stress accent of the Jacobi/Buhler type - main stress governed by the penultimate (penultimate if heavy, otherwise further back) with a secondary initial stress - a reconstructive position adopted conditionally ('if we accept') but called proved 'at any rate for Pali'…

tone_statements.quote: This very archaic system, which, indeed, includes a few variants, entirely disappeared after Panini. Although some grammarians refer to it, it is noted in no text. … it is not surprising that Middle Indian does not furnish any decisive facts in favour of a regular stress accent in the vulgar tongue. The very idea was unknown (it is noteworthy that in Pali udatta- and u\ara- are not used in any technical sense and sara- ( svara -) designates only a chant).

sources.citation: Geiger, Wilhelm. 1994 [repr. 2005]. A Pali Grammar. Translated by Batakrishna Ghosh, revised and edited by K. R. Norman. Oxford: Pali Text Society.
sources.quote: 'Nothing has been handed down to us about the nature of the Pali accent. It is, however, improbable that the ancient Indian accent was still in force. It is more likely that, as Jacobi has suggested for Pkt, the Sanskritic accent was the rule in Pali. This is suggested by the changes of vocalism in Pali, such as the weakening of a vowel after the accented syllable (in the Skt form) or its strengthening in the main accented syllable. Cf. secs. 19 foll.' (Norman's revision leaves sec. 4 substantively unchanged from the 1943 text we quote.)

sources.note: A full review of the Pali/Prakrit accent controversy as it bears on Pali verse. Vedic pitch accent ('tone') had no connection with metre; the question is whether and when a stress accent replaced the Vedic tone; Jacobi (1893, 1912-13) traced a penultimate stress accent back to Pali (accepted by Geiger and Mayrhofer), Pischel held the Vedic tone survived in (some) Prakrits, Bloch denied any accent after Panini; Warder works 'if we accept a penultimate stress accent in Pali, with a secondary initial stress' (sec. 77), says Pali 'already possessed its characteristic accent system' by the 4th c.…

tone.quote: Die ursprüngliche, musikalische Betonung, wie sie für die älteren Theile des Veda überliefert ist, scheint im epischen und klassischen Sanskrit aufgegeben worden zu sein. Auch sind uns keinerlei Nachrichten über den Accent im Pâli und in den Prâkṛit-sprachen erhalten. Und doch spricht das Vorhandensein von enclitischen Worten dafür, dass in allen diesen Sprachen des mittelalterlichen Indiens ein ausgesprochener Wortton vorhanden war, und nicht etwa schwebende Betonung obwaltete. [… Enclise passage …] Der Ictus-Accent wird, wie gesagt, nirgends geschrieben; wir lernen ihn erst in der modernen Aussprache des Sanskrit kennen.
tone.translation: The original musical accentuation … seems to have been given up in epic and classical Sanskrit. Nor has any information whatever about the accent in Pali and the Prakrit languages come down to us. And yet the existence of enclitic words argues that in all these languages of medieval India a pronounced word accent existed, and not, say, level (hovering) accentuation. … The ictus accent, as said, is nowhere written; we first come to know it in the modern pronunciation of Sanskrit.
tone.summary: Says the Vedic musical (pitch) accent seems abandoned by classical Sanskrit and argues Pali and Prakrit had a dynamic an earlier reading (stress) accent instead; no tone system for Pali is stated as such.
